Main article: [Great Smoky Mountains](/wiki/Great_Smoky_Mountains "Great Smoky Mountains")

The Great Smoky Mountains National Park protects the majority of the [Great Smoky Mountains](/wiki/Great_Smoky_Mountains "Great Smoky Mountains"), a subrange of the [Blue Ridge Mountains](/wiki/Blue_Ridge_Mountains "Blue Ridge Mountains"), which are a subrange of the [Appalachian Mountains](/wiki/Appalachian_Mountains "Appalachian Mountains"). The range runs roughly east to west, nestled between the [Bald Mountains](/wiki/Bald_Mountains "Bald Mountains") to the east, the [Plott Balsams](/wiki/Plott_Balsams "Plott Balsams") to the south, and the [Unicoi Mountains](/wiki/Unicoi_Mountains "Unicoi Mountains") to the west. The park also protects a small portion of [foothills](/wiki/Foothills "Foothills"), which separate the range from the [Ridge-and-Valley Appalachians](/wiki/Ridge-and-Valley_Appalachians "Ridge-and-Valley Appalachians") to the north. From west to east, the range gradually widens, with most of the highest mountains located in the eastern half. Elevations in the park range from about 875 feet (267 m) to 6,643 feet (2,025 m) at the summit of [Kuwohi](/wiki/Kuwohi "Kuwohi").

Kuwohi is the highest mountain in Tennessee and the third-highest mountain east of the [Mississippi River](/wiki/Mississippi_River "Mississippi River").[[12]](#cite_note-12) The park contains 16 of the "[Southern Sixers](/wiki/Southern_Sixers "Southern Sixers")"; mountains in Tennessee and North Carolina that reach elevations higher than 6,000 feet (1,800 m).[[13]](#cite_note-13) The second highest mountain in the park is [Mount Guyot](/wiki/Mount_Guyot_(Great_Smoky_Mountains) "Mount Guyot (Great Smoky Mountains)"), at an elevation of 6,621 feet (2,018 m). [Mount Le Conte](/wiki/Mount_Le_Conte_(Tennessee) "Mount Le Conte (Tennessee)"), at an elevation of 6,593 feet (2,010 m), rises 5,301 feet (1,616 m) from its base to its summit, making it the tallest mountain in the United States east of the [Rocky Mountains](/wiki/Rocky_Mountains "Rocky Mountains").[[14]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTECampbell196026-14)[[15]](#cite_note-15)

Nutter was born in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, and grew up in [West Philadelphia](/wiki/West_Philadelphia "West Philadelphia"). Raised [Catholic](/wiki/Catholic_Church "Catholic Church"), he attended elementary school at Transfiguration of Our Lord Catholic Elementary School and later [St. Joseph's Preparatory School](/wiki/St._Joseph%27s_Preparatory_School "St. Joseph's Preparatory School") in [North Philadelphia](/wiki/North_Philadelphia "North Philadelphia") where he was known affectionately as "Big Nut".[[4]](#cite_note-4)[[5]](#cite_note-5)[[6]](#cite_note-6) He graduated from [The Wharton School](/wiki/Wharton_School "Wharton School") at the [University of Pennsylvania](/wiki/University_of_Pennsylvania "University of Pennsylvania") in 1979 with a degree in business.[[7]](#cite_note-7) During his [sophomore year](/wiki/Sophomore "Sophomore") in college, he started working as a [DJ](/wiki/Disc_jockey "Disc jockey") at Club Impulse in Philadelphia, where he was known as Mix Master Mike.[[8]](#cite_note-8) After graduating from college, Nutter began to work at [Xerox](/wiki/Xerox "Xerox"), and then at an [investment banking](/wiki/Investment_banking "Investment banking") firm. While in office, Nutter occasionally worked as DJ and a singer.

Nutter, then-leader of the 52nd ward of Philadelphia, initially challenged [Democratic](/wiki/Democratic_Party_(United_States) "Democratic Party (United States)") incumbent [Ann Land](/wiki/Ann_Land "Ann Land") for a seat on the [Philadelphia City Council](/wiki/Philadelphia_City_Council "Philadelphia City Council") in 1987.[[9]](#cite_note-LandObit-9) He was unsuccessful in his initial bid but defeated Land, four years later.[[9]](#cite_note-LandObit-9)

In February 2003, Nutter was elected chairman of the [Pennsylvania Convention Center Authority Board](/wiki/Pennsylvania_Convention_Center "Pennsylvania Convention Center").[[10]](#cite_note-10)

The first [general elections](/wiki/2008_Bhutanese_general_election "2008 Bhutanese general election") for the [National Assembly](/wiki/National_Assembly_(Bhutan) "National Assembly (Bhutan)") were held on 24 March 2008. The chief contestants were the [Bhutan Peace and Prosperity Party](/wiki/Bhutan_Peace_and_Prosperity_Party "Bhutan Peace and Prosperity Party") (DPT) led by [Jigme Thinley](/wiki/Jigme_Thinley "Jigme Thinley") and the [People's Democratic Party](/wiki/People%27s_Democratic_Party_(Bhutan) "People's Democratic Party (Bhutan)") (PDP) led by [Sangay Ngedup](/wiki/Sangay_Ngedup "Sangay Ngedup"). The DPT won the elections, taking 45 out of 47 seats.[[101]](#cite_note-104) [Jigme Thinley](/wiki/Jigme_Thinley "Jigme Thinley") served as [Prime Minister](/wiki/Prime_Minister_of_Bhutan "Prime Minister of Bhutan") from 2008 to 2013.

The [People's Democratic Party](/wiki/People%27s_Democratic_Party_(Bhutan) "People's Democratic Party (Bhutan)") came to power in the [2013 elections](/wiki/2013_Bhutanese_National_Assembly_election "2013 Bhutanese National Assembly election"). It won 32 seats and 54.88% of the vote. PDP leader [Tshering Tobgay](/wiki/Tshering_Tobgay "Tshering Tobgay") served as Prime Minister from 2013 to 2018.

[Druk Nyamrup Tshogpa](/wiki/Druk_Nyamrup_Tshogpa "Druk Nyamrup Tshogpa") won the largest number of seats in the [2018 National Assembly election](/wiki/2018_Bhutanese_National_Assembly_election "2018 Bhutanese National Assembly election"), bringing [Lotay Tshering](/wiki/Lotay_Tshering "Lotay Tshering") to the premiership and Druk Nyamrup Tshogpa into the government for the first time.[[102]](#cite_note-105)

Tobgay returned to power as Prime Minister after the [2024 election](/wiki/2023%E2%80%9324_Bhutanese_National_Assembly_election "2023–24 Bhutanese National Assembly election"), with the PDP gaining 30 seats; he assumed office on 28 January 2024.[[103]](#cite_note-106)

On August 13, 2018, Anthony signed a one-year, $2.4 million veterans minimum contract with the [Houston Rockets](/wiki/Houston_Rockets "Houston Rockets") coached by his former Knicks coach, [Mike D'Antoni](/wiki/Mike_D%27Antoni "Mike D'Antoni").[[200]](#cite_note-200)[[201]](#cite_note-201)[[202]](#cite_note-stein_11152018-202) On November 15, Rockets general manager [Daryl Morey](/wiki/Daryl_Morey "Daryl Morey") announced that the team was "parting ways" with Anthony, but had not released him. He played ten games for Houston, starting twice, but he was held out of the last three for what the club called an unspecified "illness."[[202]](#cite_note-stein_11152018-202) During that absence, much of his playing time went to rookie [Gary Clark](/wiki/Gary_Clark_(basketball) "Gary Clark (basketball)").[[203]](#cite_note-203) Houston had started the season losing seven of their first 11 games. Morey said that Anthony "accepted every role" asked by D'Antoni, but that the "fit we envisioned when Carmelo chose to sign with the Rockets has not materialized; therefore we thought it was best to move on as any other outcome would have been unfair to him." D'Antoni stated that he "didn't ever want to disrespect [Anthony] and his career. He's going in the Hall of Fame."[[202]](#cite_note-stein_11152018-202)

[Michael Dell](/wiki/Michael_Dell "Michael Dell") founded Dell Computer Corporation, doing business as PC's Limited, in 1984. Dell was a student at the [University of Texas at Austin](/wiki/University_of_Texas_at_Austin "University of Texas at Austin"),[[15]](#cite_note-15) and operated the business from his off-campus dormitory room at [Dobie Center](/wiki/Dobie_Center "Dobie Center").[[16]](#cite_note-16) The start-up aimed to sell [IBM PC compatible](/wiki/IBM_PC_compatible "IBM PC compatible") computers built from stock components. Michael Dell started trading in the belief that, by selling personal computer systems directly to customers, PC's Limited could better understand customers' needs and provide the most effective computing services to meet those needs.[[17]](#cite_note-17) Dell dropped out of college upon completion of his freshman year at the University of Texas in order to focus full-time on his fledgling business, after getting about $1,000 in expansion-capital from his family.[[18]](#cite_note-delltimeline-18) As of April 2021, Dell's net worth was estimated to be over $50 billion (equivalent to $56,940,000,000 in 2024).[[19]](#cite_note-19)
